transcript.text: Thank you both for these critical updates. Ms. Shah, the lead contamination at 185 ppm exceeding our 100 ppm threshold is a serious safety concern — I have not seen that soil report yet, so I'm glad you flagged it. We absolutely cannot have students working in contaminated soil, so soil remediation must be incorporated into the plan. Mr. Ellis, the grant requirements you've outlined — 10 native species instead of 6, 6 lessons instead of 3, and the specific Tuesday/Thursday 2:30 p.m. maintenance schedule — are significant changes from the current proposal. Before I can make my final decision, I need to see a revised operating plan that incorporates all of the following: (1) removal and replacement of the top 8 inches of soil with certified clean soil per district procedure, (2) adjustment to 10 native plant species as required by the grant, (3) expansion to 6 garden-based science lessons completed by November 1, 2026, (4) the supervised maintenance schedule on Tuesdays and Thursdays at 2:30 p.m., and (5) an updated timeline that accounts for the soil remediation work before any September planting begins. Once I receive that revised plan, I can move forward with approval. Can either of you tell me whether the soil remediation timeline will impact our September start date, and do we have a budget estimate for the clean soil replacement?

transcript.text: Thank you, Dr. Morgan. I can speak to the soil remediation timeline. The soil removal and replacement work — removing the top 8 inches and bringing in certified clean soil — is a straightforward facilities project, but it does take time to schedule the contractor, perform the excavation, source and deliver the certified clean soil, and confirm it passes retesting. Based on typical timelines for this kind of work, I would estimate we need at least two to three weeks from the time we get approval to order and execute the remediation, plus a few days for post-replacement soil testing to confirm the lead levels are below the 100 ppm threshold before any planting can begin. If we get approval quickly, we should be able to complete the remediation before September, but it will tighten the timeline — we would need to start mobilizing almost immediately. As for the budget, I don't have a specific cost estimate prepared yet, but I can reach out to our usual environmental remediation contractor for a quote on the excavation and clean soil replacement. I should have that estimate within a few days. I'd also note that the revised plan should include a post-remediation soil test as a verification step before students enter the garden — that's consistent with district procedure for confirming safety after remediation.
